articles.title: Riyadh airport attack toll rises to 13 dead, including an Indian, over 300 wounded
articles.summary: An attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has killed 13 people, including an Indian national who died of injuries, and wounded more than 300. It is the second strike on a Saudi airport in as many days.
articles.body:
The death toll from the attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has risen to 13, including an Indian national who died of injuries, with more than 300 people wounded, according to the latest reporting available for this edition. The figures mark an escalation from initial reports on October 11, which had described one Indian killed and ten others injured in a strike described by officials as "completely unacceptable." Indian Express separately reported that the Indian victim had been at the airport for Umrah with family. A second attack on a Saudi airport, reported separately on October 12, killed at least one more person, suggesting the toll may still be rising as follow-on reporting comes in; this edition treats the 13-dead, 300-plus-wounded figure as the latest official count rather than a final one.

The Saudi-led coalition has attributed the strikes to Houthi forces, part of the broader escalation out of Yemen that has already disrupted commercial aviation this week. Lufthansa, Air India and IndiGo had already suspended flights to Riyadh after an earlier attack, and the Indian Embassy in Riyadh issued an advisory to Indian nationals in the kingdom. India's government response has been consistent across the week: the Ministry of External Affairs has called the attacks "completely unacceptable" and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, while reiterating India's broader position that attacks on civilian and commercial infrastructure across the West Asia conflict must stop.

For India, the human cost is now direct and specific, not abstract: an Indian citizen is confirmed dead and Indian travellers are among the wounded at one of the Gulf's busiest airports. This sits alongside two other live West Asia-linked risks to Indians this week: the Strait of Hormuz attacks that have left Indian sailors missing, and the broader disruption to Gulf aviation routes that Indian carriers rely on.

For the aviation sector specifically, a second strike on a major Saudi airport within days is a serious operational risk signal. Airlines calibrate route suspensions based on how contained an attack appears to be; a second attack so soon after the first suggests the risk is not yet contained, and more carriers may extend or add suspensions on Gulf routes serving Saudi Arabia.

Watch for an official, stabilised casualty count from Saudi or Indian authorities, any further airline route decisions, and whether King Khalid International Airport's operations are affected beyond the immediate aftermath.

articles.title: Rupee jumps nearly Re 1 as RBI's four-step 'shock therapy' chokes off dollar demand
articles.summary: The rupee surged against the dollar after the RBI rolled out four measures targeting oil-company dollar demand, speculative forex derivatives and banking liquidity. The currency is still down 6.6% this year despite the relief.
articles.body:
The rupee surged nearly Re 1 against the US dollar on Monday, opening at 95.76, up 97 paise from Friday's close of 96.73, making it the standout performer among Asian currencies that otherwise traded in a narrow range. The rally followed a weekend package of RBI measures aimed squarely at two sources of pressure on the currency: oil companies' spot-market dollar demand and corporate hedging bets that were effectively speculating on further rupee depreciation.

The RBI's intervention has four parts. First, from October 12, the RBI began meeting the entire daily dollar requirement of the three state-run oil marketing companies, Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum, through designated banks, removing their demand from the interbank spot market entirely. Nomura estimates India's monthly oil import bill averaged $16.4 billion between April and August, with these three companies accounting for about 55% of that, so the window covers a large share of one of the biggest sources of dollar demand in the economy.

Second, the RBI tightened the rules on foreign exchange derivatives. It banned the rebooking of cancelled rupee-linked derivative contracts, a practice that had let companies use "hedging" transactions for speculative positioning, and cut the threshold for undertaking forex derivative transactions without an underlying exposure from $100 million to $5 million. Companies must now certify that the same exposure has not already been hedged through another bank, closing a loophole that had allowed synthetic over-hedging across multiple banks.

Third, the RBI introduced a 20% Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve: authorised dealers must now hold a cash reserve with the RBI equal to a fifth of the rupee value of eligible forex derivative contracts above $2 million, which raises the cost of taking large speculative positions. Fourth, the central bank tightened daily cash reserve requirements for banks more broadly, draining surplus banking liquidity that had been available to fund these trades.

The relief is real but the underlying pressure has not disappeared. The rupee is still down 6.6% this year, and crude oil prices, FII outflows and weak capital flows continue to weigh on the currency even after this package. The RBI's own rupee defence, by draining liquidity and raising the cost of derivatives, is itself a tightening measure layered on top of this month's repo rate hike, so the central bank is now managing both the rate cycle and the currency with overlapping, and at times compounding, tools.

For anyone with forex exposure, whether through an import business, foreign education payments, or travel, the near-term message is that the rupee's slide has been checked by policy, not by fundamentals. Watch whether oil prices ease further, following Goldman Sachs's revised forecasts this week, and whether FII flows stabilise, which would matter more for the rupee's medium-term path than the RBI's intervention tools, which have a limited shelf life.

facts.fact: Rupee opened at 95.76/USD on 2026-10-12, up 97 paise from 96.73 close

articles.title: Drone attack on tanker carrying 11 Indian seafarers leaves two missing in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: A drone attack on the tanker MT Petro Dolphin at Sohar Anchorage left two of its eleven Indian crew members missing, after nine were rescued safely. India's government called the recurring attacks on shipping deeply concerning and demanded de-escalation.
articles.body:
A drone attack on the tanker MT Petro Dolphin at Sohar Anchorage has left two Indian seafarers missing, after nine of the eleven Indian crew members aboard were rescued and confirmed safe, according to Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal. Sonowal said in a social media post that search-and-rescue operations were actively under way, led by the local Coast Guard, and that India was "continuously coordinating with all relevant authorities to fully support the ongoing rescue efforts and ensure every possible action is taken to safely locate our missing personnel."

India's government issued a strong statement on the broader pattern behind this incident. "The safety and security of Indian seafarers remain a priority for the Government of India. The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning and risk further aggravating an already volatile situation," the statement said. It called for "immediate de-escalation and a resolution to the ongoing conflict through dialogue and diplomacy," adding that "attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease" and that freedom of navigation through international waterways "must be upheld."

This incident follows a string of attacks on shipping in the region this month, including one in which eleven Indian crew members were injured by a projectile strike on a Panama-flagged vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz, and a separate Russian drone strike that killed at least two foreign crew, including injuring an Indian national, on a Turkish-owned cargo vessel in the Black Sea. Taken together, these incidents show Indian seafarers bearing a direct, repeated human cost from both the West Asia war and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, in addition to the broader economic effects those conflicts have on oil prices and the rupee.

The stakes for India are structural, not incidental. India has grown from the world's fifth-largest to its second-largest supplier of seafarers over twelve years, with its seafarer workforce rising from 1.27 lakh to 3.23 lakh and now accounting for over 12% of the global total; the government's Mission 20% initiative aims to push that share further by 2030. Every attack on a vessel with Indian crew is therefore a direct risk to a workforce the country is actively trying to grow, not a peripheral shipping story.

Watch for confirmation on the two missing seafarers' status, whether shipping lines reroute away from Hormuz and the surrounding anchorages following this incident, and whether India's call for de-escalation gets any diplomatic traction this week.

articles.title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire', also urges Ukraine to replace Zelensky
articles.summary: Donald Trump announced an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine and urged both sides not to break it. He also said Ukraine should replace President Zelensky with a leader willing to settle the war, and the US has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, urging both sides not to break it, as part of a broader push to wind down the war. The announcement came with an unusual political demand attached: Trump also said Ukraine should replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, arguing the country needs "a new president" and that Zelensky should be replaced by a leader willing to settle the war on different terms. That comment puts Trump's diplomacy on a collision course with Kyiv's own political leadership, since Zelensky has not indicated any plan to step down.

The practical, market-relevant part of the announcement is on energy. The US separately lifted sanctions on the sale of Russian diesel in global markets, a significant policy reversal given that Western sanctions on Russian energy exports have been a central tool of pressure on Moscow since the war began. Trump has also floated wanting 4.8 million tonnes of diesel from Russia, according to separate reporting, though there are reports that a Reagan-inspired bill in Congress, framed around "Peace Through Strength," could attempt to block such a deal. US senators have separately said that elements of a Trump-Russia diesel arrangement would be illegal under existing law, signalling that this diplomatic push is contested even within Washington.

For India, the ceasefire and the sanctions reversal both matter through the oil price channel rather than direct exposure to the Russia-Ukraine conflict itself. India has been a major buyer of discounted Russian crude since Western sanctions pushed Moscow to sell at a discount; any normalisation of Russian energy exports, including diesel, could ease some of the supply-side pressure that has kept crude above $100 this year. That connects directly to this week's other big story: Goldman Sachs trimming its oil price forecasts on expectations that West Asia and Russia-linked supply disruptions gradually ease.

The geopolitics remain unsettled. An energy ceasefire is a narrower, more limited step than a full ceasefire or a peace settlement, and Trump's call for Zelensky's replacement adds a destabilising political element to what is otherwise a supply-side economic move. NATO officials have separately said Russia suffered about 50,000 casualties last month alone, a reminder that the war's human cost continues even as this narrower energy-focused de-escalation is attempted.

Watch whether Russia and Ukraine both actually observe the energy ceasefire in practice, how Kyiv responds to Trump's call for new leadership, and whether the diesel-sanctions reversal survives the legislative pushback in Washington.

articles.title: Goldman Sachs raises December 2026 Brent forecast to $90, but still well below today's $103
articles.summary: Goldman Sachs raised its December 2026 Brent oil forecast to $90 a barrel, citing supply-side risk from the West Asia war, even though that is still 13% below the current price of about $103. Its 2027 worst case puts Brent at $125 if Gulf output stays depressed.
articles.body:
Goldman Sachs has raised its December 2026 Brent crude price forecast by 6% to $90 a barrel, up from $85 earlier, citing continued supply-side risk from the West Asia war. Even the upgraded forecast sits nearly 13% below the current price of around $103 a barrel, reflecting Goldman's base case that oil supply adaptation will gradually bring prices down even as the bank nudges up its near-term number to account for a slower-than-expected fall in the risk premium, which it estimates at just over $20 today.

The bank's 2027 average Brent forecast stays unchanged at $80 a barrel, balancing downward pressure from faster Gulf supply adaptation against a risk premium that is fading more slowly than hoped. WTI, unusually cheap relative to Brent because of high US-Europe shipping costs, is forecast to average $81 in December 2026 and $73 in 2027.

The range of outcomes Goldman lays out is wide, and the drivers matter for anyone tracking India's oil import bill. Before the West Asia war began in late February, crude was trading around $70 a barrel. It spiked above $125 when the Strait of Hormuz, a transit route for close to 20% of the world's oil shipments, effectively closed for business. A gradual reopening pulled prices back toward pre-war levels before the current escalation pushed crude back up toward $100. Goldman's upside scenario has Brent averaging around $125 in 2027 if Gulf output in that year stays 5 million barrels a day below February 2026 levels, driven by damage to oil infrastructure, intensified shipping attacks or a more persistent risk premium, any of which are plausible given this week's attacks on Riyadh's airport and on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The downside scenario has Brent falling into the $60s if Gulf output instead rises 1 million barrels a day above February 2026 levels, which would require a faster resolution of the conflict than currently seems likely.

S&P Global Energy's own outlook is narrower, expecting Brent in an $80-$100 range through 2027, with fourth-quarter 2026 global demand estimated at 80.2 million barrels a day, 4.7 million barrels a day below the same period a year earlier, reflecting both the price effect and refining bottlenecks caused by damage in both the Russia-Ukraine and West Asia conflicts.

For India, which imports most of its crude, the practical takeaway is that forecasters are not expecting a quick return to pre-war oil prices. Even the more optimistic scenarios keep Brent above $80 through next year, which keeps pressure on the rupee, the current account and domestic fuel pricing, all three of which are already under strain this month.

articles.title: HCL Tech expected to post double-digit profit growth in Q2, helped by Guardian Life ramp-up
articles.summary: HCL Tech is expected to report low-to-mid double-digit profit and revenue growth for Q2 FY27, helped by the Guardian Life deal and recent acquisitions. The board will also consider a third interim dividend.
articles.body:
HCL Technologies is expected to post profit and revenue growth in the low-to-mid double digits for the second quarter of FY27, when it reports results on Monday, October 12, according to brokerage previews. The board will also consider a third interim dividend for the year alongside the results; the company has already paid two cumulative dividends totalling Rs 36 this fiscal.

Brokerage estimates vary somewhat but point the same direction. Kotak Institutional Equities expects adjusted net profit growth of 15.1% year-on-year to Rs 4,901.3 crore, on revenue growth of 12.7% to Rs 36,012.8 crore, with the acquisitions of HPE's Telco Solutions business and Jaspersoft contributing 110 basis points to revenue. Axis Direct's estimate is similar in direction, projecting 11% revenue growth to Rs 35,443 crore and 15.9% profit growth to Rs 4,910 crore. Jefferies expects 2.7% quarter-on-quarter constant-currency revenue growth, including about 100 basis points of inorganic contribution from the acquisitions, with Services growing 2.5% and Software 4% on the same basis; in rupee terms, it sees 11.9% topline growth.

Margins are expected to hold broadly steady. Jefferies forecasts an EBIT margin of 17.6%, up 25 basis points year-on-year, while Kotak expects a 50-basis-point quarter-on-quarter improvement, though it notes that rupee-depreciation benefits will be partly offset by margin dilution from the recent acquisitions. On deal flow, Kotak expects total contract value of $3.75 billion, driven by a Euro 1 billion mega deal and a large deal from Guardian Life, the insurance client whose ramp-up is a key driver of this quarter's growth story.

Guidance is the number investors will watch most closely. Kotak expects HCL Tech to raise its revenue growth guidance to 3-4% from 1-4% earlier, with the acquisitions contributing about 100 basis points of that, while organic constant-currency growth guidance stays broadly unchanged at 2-3%. Jefferies, by contrast, expects HCL Tech to narrow its FY27 services revenue growth guidance by 50 basis points to 2-4%, and expects the company to retain its 17.5-18.5% EBIT margin band, albeit toward the lower end.

This result lands in the same week as TCS's own Q2 numbers and the broader Nifty IT rally, so HCL Tech's guidance commentary on AI-led deflation in the services business, alongside its deal pipeline, will be read as a second data point on whether Indian IT's AI transition is translating into real revenue growth or just margin pressure. As this is a pre-results preview based on brokerage estimates, the actual numbers, once reported, should be checked against these projections rather than assumed.
sources_checked: Business Standard (brokerage estimates: Kotak, Jefferies, Axis Direct)

articles.title: India moves to stockpile critical minerals as China's processing dominance exposes supply risk
articles.summary: India is finalising a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme to guard against supply disruptions, as the country remains almost entirely import-dependent for processed critical minerals. China controls 90% of global critical mineral processing capacity.
articles.body:
India is finalising a policy to stockpile critical minerals, addressing a stark vulnerability: the country has little processing capacity for these minerals and is close to 100% import-dependent for most of them, while China controls roughly 90% of global critical mineral processing capacity and has at times used that position as leverage during trade tensions.

The policy flows from the National Critical Minerals Mission, which has proposed a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme covering at least five critical minerals, designed specifically to mitigate the risk of supply-chain disruptions and ensure availability for domestic needs during emergencies. The government has committed Rs 500 crore to the mission over a seven-year period, from 2024-25 to 2030-31. A government document on the mission states that "a joint initiative between central PSUs or with private companies shall be institutionalised to develop a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme."

India's efforts to secure these minerals have run into real obstacles on the overseas side. The government's flagship overseas acquisition vehicle, Khanij Bidesh India Limited (KABIL), has struggled to expand its footprint in mineral-rich countries including Australia, Vietnam, Mali and Chile, where proposed investments in extraction projects have stalled or fallen through. The one clear success so far is in Argentina, where KABIL has acquired five lithium brine blocks in Catamarca province.

On the domestic processing side, India is trying to build capacity rather than rely solely on stockpiling. The government has identified four states, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Gujarat and Maharashtra, to host critical mineral processing plants, with each state developed as a complete ecosystem around a particular mineral: Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh are focused on rare earth processing, while Odisha and Maharashtra are set to focus on nickel and lithium respectively.

The strategic logic connects directly to broader supply-chain anxieties visible elsewhere this week, from chip-export controls to oil-supply disruption from the West Asia war: India is trying to reduce single points of dependency across multiple critical input categories at once. For a country betting heavily on EV manufacturing, electronics and renewable energy, where critical minerals like lithium, cobalt and rare earths are essential inputs, the stockpile programme and the domestic processing push are two sides of the same strategic bet: that global supply chains for these minerals will remain contested, and that India needs its own buffer rather than relying entirely on open markets.

Watch for the stockpile programme's formal notification, which minerals are prioritised first, and whether any of the stalled KABIL projects in Australia, Vietnam, Mali or Chile are revived.

articles.title: TSMC poised for sixth straight record-profit quarter as AI chip demand keeps surging
articles.summary: TSMC is expected to report a 65% surge in third-quarter profit, driven by AI chip and advanced packaging demand. Its market cap is now almost double Samsung's, and it is weighing a further US expansion in Texas.
articles.body:
TSMC, the world's largest manufacturer of advanced AI chips, is expected to report a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings on Thursday, with a projected 65% surge in third-quarter net profit to T$746.3 billion ($23.4 billion), according to an LSEG SmartEstimate compiled from 16 analysts. Any result above T$706.56 billion would mark the company's highest-ever quarterly net income and its 11th straight quarter of profit growth. TSMC already posted a 50% year-on-year revenue rise last week, beating market forecasts and hitting a new record.

The demand driver is consistent: strong appetite for TSMC's advanced AI chipmaking capacity and its CoWoS advanced packaging technology, which has pushed the company's market capitalisation to around $2.1 trillion, almost double that of South Korean rival Samsung Electronics, and cemented its position as a key supplier to both Nvidia and Apple. Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan expects TSMC to raise its full-year revenue growth guidance to the low-to-mid 40% range, up from its current guidance of more than 40%, driven by strong demand for its 3-nanometre chips.

The bigger strategic question for this earnings call is expansion. TSMC is already investing $265 billion to build chip factories in Arizona, including an additional $100 billion announced in July, and Reuters reported in September that the company was evaluating a potential investment in Texas as well. Tesla chief executive Elon Musk has said his companies would build and operate the Terafab AI chip complex, with TSMC potentially subleasing part of it. Analysts are split on urgency: Morgan Stanley's Chan argues a Texas expansion could become necessary within five years given customer demand and limited remaining space at the Arizona site, while Morningstar's Phelix Lee sees limited urgency, noting that some of TSMC's planned Arizona fabs have not even been built yet.

This result matters for the broader AI investment cycle that touches this edition's other stories: TCS and HCL Tech are both betting on AI-driven IT demand, Nvidia is in talks over Reflection AI, and the IMF has separately said AI investment is boosting growth prospects for Asian economies. TSMC sits upstream of almost all of that activity, since it manufactures the chips that power the AI infrastructure everyone else is building on top of. A sixth straight record quarter would be strong evidence that the AI capex cycle, which some commentators (including billionaire investor Ray Dalio) have warned could be heading toward a bubble, is still being backed by real, growing chip demand rather than speculation alone.

Watch the actual results and the fourth-quarter guidance call at 0600 GMT on Thursday, and specifically whether management addresses the Texas expansion question directly.

articles.title: GST Council endorses uniform 5% tax on Ola, Uber, Swiggy, Zomato and e-commerce platforms
articles.summary: The GST Council has endorsed a uniform 5% tax treatment for ride-hailing and delivery platforms regardless of how their businesses are structured, a senior CBIC official said. The move closes a long-running ambiguity over how aggregator models are taxed.
articles.body:
The GST Council has endorsed a uniform tax treatment of 5% for platform operators including Ola, Uber, Swiggy, Zomato, Amazon and Flipkart, regardless of how their individual businesses are structured, according to Sanjay Mangal, a CBIC member for GST. The statement resolves a long-running point of ambiguity in how India's indirect-tax system treats platform and aggregator business models, which have historically varied in whether they act as a marketplace, a principal seller or a pure service intermediary.

The significance of "regardless of business model" is specific: platform companies have previously structured their operations in different ways partly to manage their GST exposure, with the tax treatment depending on technical questions about whether the platform is deemed to be supplying the service itself or merely facilitating a transaction between a consumer and an independent driver, restaurant or seller. A uniform 5% rate removes that structuring incentive and gives both the tax administration and the platforms themselves more certainty on compliance.

This decision comes in the same week as the GST Council's broader reform package on arrest powers, prosecution thresholds and refund timelines, reported earlier this month, which focused on procedure and enforcement rather than specific sector rates. The platform-taxation decision is a narrower, sector-specific move, but it affects a large and fast-growing part of the consumer economy: ride-hailing, food delivery and e-commerce collectively touch hundreds of millions of Indian transactions a month.

For the affected companies, a clear and uniform rate is generally welcome even when it closes a previously favourable interpretation, because it removes legal and compliance uncertainty that can affect fundraising, IPO readiness and investor confidence. For consumers, the direct effect depends on how much of the tax was already being passed through in pricing versus absorbed by the platforms; a clarified rate does not necessarily mean a price change, since it may simply formalise what many platforms were effectively already charging.

For drivers, delivery workers and sellers on these platforms, who are often the subject of separate debates about gig-work classification and earnings, this decision is specifically about the platform's own tax liability, not about their individual income tax or GST registration requirements, which remain governed by separate rules.

Watch for the Council's formal notification of the rate and its effective date, and whether any of the affected companies adjust consumer-facing pricing in response.
sources_checked: Mint (CBIC member for GST, Sanjay Mangal)

categories: Economy & Banking bodies (RBI, SEBI, NABARD, IBRD, IMF, etc.)

facts.fact: GST Council endorsed uniform 5% tax rate for platform/aggregator operators

articles.title: Nvidia in talks to deepen investment in, or acquire, coding startup Reflection AI
articles.summary: Nvidia is reportedly in early-stage talks to invest further in or acquire Reflection AI, an open-source coding startup it has already backed with $800 million. A deal could take the form of an acqui-hire rather than a full acquisition.
articles.body:
Nvidia is in talks to deepen its investment in open-source startup Reflection AI, or to acquire it outright, the Financial Times reported, citing people with direct knowledge of the matter. The talks are at an early stage, and a deal could take several forms, including a so-called acqui-hire arrangement in which Nvidia would hire Reflection's staff and license its technology rather than pursue a full acquisition, a structure that could help avoid a lengthy regulatory review. An agreement could be reached within weeks, according to the report, though the discussions could still fall apart; Reuters said it could not immediately verify the FT's reporting, and neither company responded to requests for comment outside regular business hours.

Nvidia is already a significant backer of Reflection AI, having invested $800 million in the company. Reflection was founded in 2024 by Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, both former DeepMind researchers, and builds tools that automate software development, one of the fastest-growing application areas for AI. Laskin told CNBC in April that the company was raising fresh capital at a pre-money valuation of $25 billion. This week, Reflection launched its first open-weight model, called Beam, as it tries to compete in coding and agentic AI tasks against lower-cost Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Kimi.

The strategic logic for Nvidia is straightforward: the company's core business is selling the chips that power AI training and inference, and a deeper stake in, or ownership of, a leading coding-AI startup gives it both a reference customer for its own hardware and a foothold in one of the application layers that is driving demand for that hardware in the first place. It mirrors a broader pattern this year of chip and infrastructure companies moving up the stack into applications, rather than staying purely as hardware suppliers.

This story sits alongside two other AI-industry threads in this edition: TSMC's expected record profit, which shows strong demand at the hardware-manufacturing layer, and the competitive pressure from lower-cost Chinese models that Reflection is explicitly positioning against. If Nvidia does acquire or deepen its stake in Reflection, it would be one more data point in the consolidation of AI infrastructure and applications around a small number of very large, well-capitalised players.

Watch for confirmation of a deal structure and valuation in the coming weeks, and for Reflection's own commercial traction with its new Beam model.

articles.title: US quietly reverses course, lets AI developers share models with UK safety testers again
articles.summary: The Trump administration reversed an earlier position and will again allow OpenAI and Anthropic to give Britain's AI Security Institute early access to models for safety testing. The shift comes as Trump's own AI task force asks developers to report security incidents.
articles.body:
American AI developers can once again give the British government early access to AI models for safety testing without running into trouble with the Trump administration, according to a report in the Telegraph. The Trump administration had previously asked developers including OpenAI and Anthropic not to share new AI models with Britain's AI Security Institute before public release; that position has now been reversed, the newspaper said. Spokespersons for Trump, OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.

Britain's AI Security Institute was set up after the world's first AI safety summit in 2023, and it tests the most advanced AI models to evaluate their capabilities and the risk of misuse before they reach the public. The earlier US request effectively cut off one channel of independent, pre-release safety scrutiny for frontier models, so reversing it restores a degree of international cooperation on AI safety testing that had been curtailed.

The shift is notable because it runs somewhat against the administration's broader posture. Trump has repeatedly dismissed calls for binding safety requirements on AI developers, arguing that heavy regulation would hand an advantage to China in the AI race. That stance appears to be shifting, at least partially: Trump's newly launched AI task force, the Super Intelligence Force reported on earlier this month, said on Friday that developers must report security incidents involving their AI models, which is itself a modest regulatory step even if short of binding safety requirements.

Read together with this week's other AI-safety stories, including Anthropic's own IPO prospectus warning about catastrophic AI risks and separate reports of fired OpenAI safety researchers accusing the company of a "chilling" effect on internal safety work, this reversal suggests that international and bilateral AI-safety cooperation is quietly continuing even as the loudest public debate in the US remains focused on deregulation and competitiveness with China.

For a reader tracking AI governance, the practical takeaway is that policy here is less settled than public statements suggest, and specific administrative decisions, like this one on UK model-sharing, can move independently of, and sometimes contrary to, the administration's headline rhetoric. Watch for whether other allied governments' AI safety institutes get similar access, and for the Super Intelligence Force's first substantive policy outputs.

articles.title: Delta Air Lines cuts 2026 earnings forecast as Q3 profit misses estimates
articles.summary: Delta Air Lines lowered its 2026 earnings guidance to $5.10-$5.60 per share, sharply below the $6.50-$7.50 range it had reaffirmed in July. Shares dipped after the Q3 results missed analyst expectations.
articles.body:
Delta Air Lines cut its 2026 earnings forecast sharply, now expecting adjusted earnings of $5.10 to $5.60 per share for the year, down from the $6.50 to $7.50 range it had reaffirmed as recently as July. The guidance cut came alongside third-quarter results that missed analyst estimates, and the stock dipped 1.72% in response.

A guidance cut of this size, roughly 20-30% off the midpoint of the prior range, signals that Delta's own management sees a materially weaker earnings environment ahead than it did just a few months ago. While the specific drivers behind Delta's revision are not detailed in the reporting available for this edition, the timing lines up with broader pressures hitting the airline industry globally this quarter: elevated and volatile jet fuel costs tied to the West Asia conflict and crude prices sitting above $100 a barrel, alongside demand uncertainty tied to the US economic and interest-rate picture.

This is a useful read-across for India's own aviation sector, even though Delta is a US carrier. Indian airlines are grappling with some of the same cost pressure: IndiGo has already raised its fuel charge this month in response to rising fuel prices, pushing airfares higher on domestic routes, and Air India and IndiGo have both had to suspend Gulf routes to Riyadh following the Houthi attacks on Saudi airports. Fuel costs and route disruption are hitting airlines on both sides of the world simultaneously, driven by the same underlying oil-price and geopolitical risk.

For investors, a major US carrier cutting guidance this sharply is also a signal worth weighing against the generally more optimistic tone elsewhere in markets this week, such as the Nifty IT rally or TCS's results. Airlines are a classically cyclical, fuel-cost-sensitive business, so Delta's cut is one more data point suggesting that higher-for-longer oil prices are starting to show up in corporate guidance, not just in commodity markets.

Watch for other major airlines' Q3 results and guidance in the coming weeks, and whether any Indian carriers follow with their own guidance revisions tied to fuel costs.

articles.title: Super Micro-linked contractor pleads guilty in $2.5 billion scheme to divert Nvidia AI chips to China
articles.summary: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer pleaded guilty to illegally exporting servers with advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. US prosecutors had charged him and two others, including a Super Micro co-founder, with diverting about $2.5 billion worth of restricted AI technology.
articles.body:
A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer has pleaded guilty to a scheme to illegally export computer servers containing advanced Nvidia AI chips to China, according to a court filing. Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun entered his guilty plea on Thursday in US District Court in Manhattan. In March, US prosecutors had charged Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder of the company, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. Super Micro did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, and its shares were down marginally in extended trading.

According to the indictment, the alleged scheme began around 2024, with the defendants using a company in Southeast Asia as a pass-through entity to conceal the identity of the China-based end customers actually receiving the equipment. The servers in question contained Nvidia's B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, all of which are on the US Commerce Control List and subject to export restrictions that require a licence for sale to China, specifically because of their relevance to advanced AI training and national security applications.

This case is a concrete example of the broader US-China contest over AI dominance that runs through several of this week's stories. Washington has steadily tightened export controls on advanced AI chips and server systems, citing national security concerns, while both countries continue investing heavily in AI as a technology seen as critical to economic growth as well as military and cybersecurity capability. A guilty plea in a case of this scale, involving a Super Micro co-founder among the co-defendants, is a reminder that enforcement of these export controls is not just rhetorical; the Justice Department is actively prosecuting large-scale diversion schemes, and this plea is likely to be used as leverage or precedent in the remaining defendants' cases.

For companies in the AI hardware supply chain, including any with operations or partners in Southeast Asia that touch chip logistics, this case is a reminder that export-control compliance is now a live enforcement risk, not just a paperwork requirement. Watch for sentencing details for Sun and for how the remaining co-defendants' cases, including the Super Micro co-founder's, proceed.

briefs.text: The IMF said AI investment is boosting growth prospects for Asian economies. The assessment adds an official institutional voice to the debate over how much AI capex is actually lifting real growth versus inflating asset valuations.

Jefferies assessed whether the RBI's higher cash reserve requirement will hit HDFC Bank, SBI and other bank stocks. Tighter liquidity requirements squeeze bank margins, which is why banking stocks are a direct read-through of this month's RBI tightening moves.

Asset manager Amundi's India arm said an end to the Iran war would be a turning point for the Indian market. The view ties directly into this week's oil-price and rupee stories, since a durable de-escalation is the clearest path to lower crude and a stronger currency.

Indian debt funds are set to extend a $4.5 billion bond selloff following the RBI's policy shift to a tighter stance. Rising yields on the back of the rate hike make existing bonds less attractive, pushing funds to keep selling.
China's trade restrictions on services exporters are under review, according to a new report. Any easing or tightening would matter for India's own competing services-export sector.

India's food industry has warned of a supply shock linked to a forming Super El Nino weather pattern. The warning adds to existing inflation risk from high energy prices and earlier patchy-monsoon concerns that fed into this month's RBI rate decision.

The statistics ministry has proposed a common framework for calculating state-level GDP figures. A standardised methodology would make state growth numbers more comparable, addressing a long-standing data-quality complaint among economists.
Sequoia-backed chip startup Nuvacore is raising funds at a valuation of about $2.5 billion. The round adds to a wave of large private AI-chip funding rounds this year.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella argued that the most trustworthy AI systems are the ones that demand the least inherent trust in any single model. The framing favours layered safety checks over simply trusting a more capable model outright.

India Mobile Congress 2026 concluded with a focus on agricultural AI, 5G automation and last-mile connectivity. The themes point to where Indian telecom and AI investment is heading beyond the usual enterprise and consumer use cases.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal argued that every H-1B visa the US does not grant is effectively a win for India, since it keeps skilled talent at home. The comment follows this month's PERM suspension and broader US immigration tightening affecting Indian IT firms.
A draft steel policy targets 604 million tonnes of capacity by 2047. The target signals how aggressively India plans to scale heavy industry capacity over the next two decades.
Korean AI-linked stocks that were a hot trade are now struggling to find buyers. The cooling is a regional data point for the broader debate over whether AI-stock enthusiasm is overextended.

Iran called the latest US response to its proposal 'insufficient', suggesting talks aimed at de-escalating the West Asia conflict remain stuck. The stalemate keeps the oil-price risk premium elevated.
US senators said a Trump-Russia diesel deal would be illegal under existing law. The objection is a direct challenge to the sanctions reversal reported alongside Trump's announced energy ceasefire.

A report examined why Saudi air defences are struggling to repel repeated Houthi attacks on airports and infrastructure. The analysis is relevant background to this week's second attack on a Saudi airport in as many days.

Supply-chain shifts and policy incentives are fuelling a boom in Indian manufacturing startups. The trend connects to the broader push for domestic capacity in sectors like critical minerals and semiconductors.

Airport hospitality firm Encalm is looking beyond lounges to build a Rs 5,000 crore hospitality business. The expansion is a concrete example of ancillary revenue growth in India's airport ecosystem, relevant for anyone tracking aviation-adjacent careers.

Outgoing Paramount CEO David Zaslav is set for a $606 million payday from Paramount's Warner Bros takeover. The scale of the payout has drawn attention as a case study in executive compensation around major media mergers.
North Korea fired missiles after issuing a border breach warning. The move adds to regional security tension in East Asia.
A New York judge blocked a Trump administration policy on taxpayer-funded government advertising. The ruling is a domestic US legal check on executive action.

Iranian official Mohsen Rezaei said Washington has accepted some conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but called the response insufficient overall. Any reopening would matter directly for oil prices and the shipping risks Indian seafarers currently face.

A NATO official said Russia suffered about 50,000 casualties last month in the Ukraine war. The figure underscores the war's continuing human cost even as a narrower energy ceasefire is being attempted.
A power bank incident forced a Chennai-bound IndiGo flight to divert and land in Hyderabad. The incident adds to a string of lithium-battery-related safety events airlines are dealing with this year.
Crypto exchange WazirX said its futures trading volume jumped 236% in the third quarter as it expanded AI tools. The growth is notable given the broader regulatory caution around crypto in India.

Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the regulator will issue closing auction session guidelines within a week. The rules will affect how the final minutes of trading are governed on Indian exchanges.

Prediction market Kalshi is investigating suspicious trades tied to a pick for Trump's press secretary, according to a report. The probe raises questions about insider trading risk on prediction markets tied to political appointments.
